text:
# How the Bicycle Changed the World

What has two wheels, no engine, and changed how millions of people live? The bicycle took about 70 years to become the machine we ride today, and every step solved a real problem.

## A machine with no pedals

In 1817, Karl Drais built his invention, a wooden frame known as the dandy horse. It had two wheels in a line, handlebars and a seat, but no pedals. Riders pushed the ground with their feet, a bit like a scooter. Drais rode about 13 kilometres in under an hour.

Even without pedals, the first bicycle beat walking.

## Pedals, chains and air

In the 1860s, French makers added pedals to the front wheel. The ride was so rough that these bikes got the nickname boneshakers. In the 1870s, the front wheel grew huge for more speed, and falls became common.

The fix came in 1885, when John Kemp Starley sold the Rover, with two wheels of the same size and a chain to the back wheel. In 1888, John Boyd Dunlop made an air-filled tyre.

Chains and air-filled tyres made cycling safe and comfortable.

## Freedom on two wheels

In the 1890s, cheap bicycles gave ordinary people their own transport for the first time. Susan B. Anthony said the bicycle had "done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world."

Today there are about 1 billion bicycles in the world. In the Netherlands, about 27% of trips are made by bicycle.

A cheap machine gave millions of people the freedom to travel.

## Conclusion

The bicycle shows how small improvements add up. A wooden toy became one of the cleanest ways to travel, and it still runs on nothing but human energy.
